signals.see: Sorted array + "find a pair/triple summing to target"
Sorted, or "smallest/largest x that works", or "find position"
"Contiguous subarray/substring" + a constraint (≤ k distinct, sum, longest/shortest)
"Subarray sums to k" / many range-sum queries
"Next greater/smaller", spans, histogram, temperatures
"Max/min in every window of size k"
Intervals: "merge/insert overlapping" (→ a set)
Intervals: "max that fit" / "min to remove" / "min arrows" (→ a number)
Linked list: "cycle?", "middle", "find the duplicate number"
Linked list: "reverse", reorder, palindrome
Linked list: head may change (insert/delete at front, merge)
"Connected?", "how many groups/components", cycle in an undirected graph
"Prerequisites", "ordering", "can you finish" (a DAG)
"Shortest # of steps" / "level by level" (unweighted)
Tree property that depends on children (height, balanced, diameter)
BST "sorted output" or "validate"
"All subsets / permutations / combinations", "find every way"
Overlapping subproblems / "min/max/count ways" with optimal substructure
"Kth largest / smallest", "top k", "k closest"
"Majority element" (> n/2 or > n/3)
Array of `1..n`, find the missing / duplicate
"Running median" of a stream
"Kth largest" and you want O(n) average, no full sort

techniques.name: Backtracking
techniques.whenToUse: Enumerate every candidate by extending a partial choice one step, recursing, then undoing it — the answer is the set of all arrangements, not a single best one.
signals: "All subsets / permutations / combinations", "find every way"
Explicit Item Resequencing
Structural Choice Sequence Steps

picking.feature: The output is EVERY valid arrangement (all subsets / permutations / combinations), so exponential work is unavoidable — choose, recurse, un-choose.

notWhen.because: the question is a count / min / max over choices and the same sub-state recurs — cache states instead of enumerating every path

variants.title: Permutations Pattern
variants.when: Finding every possible layout variation of an items list where ordering determines unique results.

complexity.why: n! complete permutations, each copied in O(n); the path and the recursion depth are both O(n) (the output list itself is not counted)

variants.title: Combinations and Subsets Pattern
variants.when: Generating all variations of variable-length groupings where sequence arrangement is irrelevant.

complexity.why: 2ⁿ subsets, each copied in up to O(n); recursion depth never exceeds n

pitfalls: Appending the mutable path itself instead of a copy — every stored result later mutates into the same list
Permutations restart `i` at 0 with a used-check; subsets start at `start_index` — mixing the two loop bounds yields duplicates or missing sets
Forgetting to undo the choice after the recursive call (the `pop`) — the path leaks into sibling branches
Skipping duplicates needs a sort first plus `if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue` — without the sort the check is meaningless

techniques.name: Binary Search
techniques.whenToUse: Binary search works on any monotonic yes/no boundary, not just sorted arrays. Use it when you can test a candidate answer cheaply and the search space is sorted or monotonically structured.
signals: Sorted, or "smallest/largest x that works", or "find position"

picking.feature: A yes/no predicate that flips exactly once across the search space — a sorted array, or a monotonic answer space like "can finish at speed k" — so halving the range is safe.

notWhen.because: you need a PAIR of positions meeting a condition, not one boundary — sorted input alone doesn't make it a binary search
the thing you want is a contiguous run whose validity changes as it grows, not a single index

variants.title: Exact Value Search
variants.when: Find an exact target value in the array

complexity.why: each step halves the candidate range; only two indices are held

variants.title: Minimum Boundary Search (First True Position)
variants.when: Find the leftmost position where a monotonic predicate is true
variants.code:
if is_valid(mid):  # Predicate is true
    r = mid  # Keep mid as candidate, search left
else:  # Predicate is false
    l = mid + 1  # Move past mid, search right

complexity.why: log n probes, each paying one predicate check costing c; `r = mid` keeps the valid candidate inside the range

variants.title: Maximum Boundary Search (Last True Position)
variants.when: Find the rightmost position where a monotonic predicate is true
variants.code:
if is_valid(mid):  # Predicate is true
    l = mid  # Keep mid as candidate, search right
else:  # Predicate is false
    r = mid - 1  # Move before mid, search left

complexity.why: mirror of the minimum form — log n probes, each paying the predicate; `l = mid` keeps the last valid candidate

pitfalls: left <= right (find exact) vs left < right (find boundary) — mixing them causes off-by-one
right = mid vs right = mid − 1 — if mid can be the answer, use right = mid
Max-boundary form: with `l = mid` compute `mid = (l + r + 1) // 2`, or the loop never terminates when `l == r − 1`
Rotated sorted array: identify which half is sorted first, then decide which side the target is on
Integer overflow on mid — (left + right) // 2 is safe in Python; in Java/C++ use left + (right − left) / 2

keyProblems.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array

techniques.name: Dummy Node (Sentinel)
techniques.whenToUse: A fake node placed before the head of a linked list so that operations on the head need no special-casing. Also the backbone of "build a new list" (merge/partition) via a dummy + tail.
signals: deleting or inserting at the head (head may change)
building a new list (merge two lists, partition, add two numbers)
you catch yourself writing `if node == head: ...` special cases

picking.feature: The head itself might be removed, replaced, or not exist yet — a sentinel before it makes every splice the same `prev.next` rewrite, with no head special-case.

notWhen.because: the head only MOVES (reversal returns `prev`); a sentinel adds nothing when no node is spliced in or out
you are only reading positions (middle, cycle), not rewiring links

variants.title: Template
variants.code:
dummy = ListNode(0)
dummy.next = head
prev = dummy
# ... walk prev/curr, splice via prev.next ...
return dummy.next          # NOT head — head may have changed

complexity.why: one walk over the list; the sentinel is the single extra node

variants.title: Build-a-list variant (merge / partition)

complexity.why: each node of either input is attached exactly once; the sentinel and `tail` are the only extras — no new nodes

pitfalls: Returning `head` instead of `dummy.next` — if the head was removed/changed, `head` is stale.
Forgetting to advance `prev`/`tail` — leaves the list mis-wired.
Not terminating the tail (`tail.next = None`) in partition-style splits → accidental cycle.

keyProblems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II

techniques.name: Dynamic Programming
techniques.whenToUse: The question asks for one number about all the ways to do something (how many, the fewest, the most, or whether any works), and the same sub-question comes up through many different paths. Solve each sub-question once, store it, and build the answer from the stored values.
signals: "How many ways", "minimum / maximum", "is it possible", over a sequence of choices
The rest of the problem depends only on where you are now, not on how you got there

picking.feature: The answer is a single count / min / max / yes-no, and a state such as "standing at index i" is reached by many different paths, so each state is solved once instead of once per path.

variants.title: Fixed Jumps (top-down)
variants.when: each state reads a constant set of other states, one per move, such as `i + 1` and `i + 2`.

complexity.why: n + 1 states, each combining k fixed moves at O(1) per move; the memo and the recursion chain are both n + 1 deep

variants.title: Fixed Jumps (bottom-up)
variants.when: the same shape, without recursion: no stack-depth limit, and the table can shrink to the last few entries.
variants.code:
def solve(n):
    table = [INVALID] * (n + MAX_STEP + 1)  # slots past n hold the invalid value
    table[n] = BASE                         # base case, seeded before the loop
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):          # fill order: i reads i + step, so go right to left
        table[i] = COMBINE(table[i + step] for step in STEPS)
    return table[0]

complexity.why: one pass over n states with k reads each; when only the last MAX_STEP entries are read, keep that many variables instead for O(1) space

variants.title: Any-Length Piece (top-down)
variants.when: each move cuts a piece `s[i:j]` of any length off the front of what is left, and the piece has to pass a check.

complexity.why: n + 1 states, each trying up to n pieces with a check costing c; the memo and the recursion chain are both n + 1 deep

variants.title: Any-Length Piece (bottom-up)
variants.when: the same shape, without recursion.

complexity.why: n entries, each scanning up to n pieces with a check costing c; one table of n + 1

pitfalls: No invalid-move case: a move that jumps past the end never reaches the base case and recurses until the stack limit
Returning the combined value without storing it in the memo, so the lookup never finds anything and every repeat is solved again
A state that leaves out a variable the answer depends on (two situations share one key) or keeps one it does not (`path`), which leaves the cache wrong or useless
Bottom-up fill order that reads an entry before it is filled
Pricing a memoized function as its tree without the memo: count distinct states × work per state instead

techniques.name: Fast & Slow Pointer
techniques.whenToUse: Two pointers moving at different speeds through a sequence (usually a linked list). The speed gap is what detects cycles, finds the middle, and locates positions relative to the end — all in one pass, O(1) space.
signals: does this linked list have a cycle?
find the middle of the list
find where the cycle begins
"find the duplicate number" in an array of `1..n` (it's a cycle in disguise)
palindrome linked list (find middle, reverse half)

picking.feature: The question is about POSITION in a chain you cannot index — middle, cycle, cycle entry — and a 2:1 speed gap answers it in one pass with no extra memory.

notWhen.because: you need to CHANGE the links, not locate a node — though reversal often follows a middle-find (palindrome, reorder)
the input is an indexable array — opposite-ends or separation pointers apply; fast/slow exists for chains you can only walk

variants.title: Template — the two-speed walk
variants.code:
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:      # guard BOTH: fast.next.next needs both non-null
    slow = slow.next           # 1 step
    fast = fast.next.next      # 2 steps
    # if cycle: they will eventually meet (fast == slow)
# if no cycle: fast falls off the end; slow is at the MIDDLE

complexity.why: fast reaches the end (or the meeting point) in at most n/2 iterations; two pointers only

variants.title: Finding the cycle's start (Floyd, phase 2)
variants.code:
slow2 = head
while slow2 != slow:
    slow2 = slow2.next
    slow = slow.next
return slow                    # entrance of the cycle

complexity.why: phase 2 walks at most n further steps before the pointers meet at the entrance; still two pointers

pitfalls: Loop guard — `while fast and fast.next` is mandatory; `fast = fast.next.next` dereferences two levels. (This is the exact 141 sticking point.)
Even vs odd length — where `slow` lands as "middle" differs by one; decide if you want the first or second middle and adjust the guard (`while fast.next and fast.next.next` gives the first middle).
Comparing nodes, not values — cycle detection compares node identity (`fast is slow`), not `.val`.

techniques.name: Floyd–Warshall — All-Pairs Shortest Paths
techniques.whenToUse: You need all pairs, n is small (≲ 400), or the graph is dense
signals: "shortest distance between every pair" / "for each node, something about all other nodes"
a small `n` (≤ ~400) paired with a weighted graph — especially when `n` is suspiciously small next to a large-sounding problem
a per-node aggregate that needs all its distances before it can be computed (a count, a max, a sum)
weights that may be negative, in an all-pairs setting

picking.feature: All pairs, small or dense graph

notWhen.because: One source, non-negative weights
One source, negative weights allowed
the graph is unweighted (or every edge costs the same) — plain BFS gives shortest paths in O(V + E) without any shortest-path machinery
All pairs, large sparse graph, non-negative — n × Dijkstra wins over O(n³)

variants.title: The procedure
variants.when: let one node at a time become a legal stopover

complexity.why: Three nested loops, each over all n nodes; every (k, i, j) triple is one constant-time comparison, independent of edge count (time). The table; in-place updating means no second copy (space).

pitfalls: `float('inf')` is safe to add in Python — `inf + inf` is `inf`, no overflow. In a fixed-width integer language use a sentinel like `1e9` and guard against `sentinel + sentinel` wrapping.
`dist[i][i] = 0` must be seeded, or the "route through k" candidate misbehaves and the §3 frozen-row argument breaks.
Undirected graphs need both directions written at seed time: `dist[u][v]` and `dist[v][u]`.
Parallel edges between the same pair: keep the minimum, don't overwrite blindly. (1334 guarantees distinct pairs, so it doesn't bite there — but it will elsewhere.)
Negative cycles, if the problem allows negative weights: after the run, `dist[i][i] < 0` for any `i` means `i` sits on a negative cycle.
The three loops are `k, i, j` in that order. Say it out loud before writing them.

keyProblems.title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance

techniques.name: In-Place Linked List Reversal
techniques.whenToUse: Reverse a list (or sublist) by rewiring `next` pointers — O(1) extra space, no new nodes.
signals: "reverse the list" / "reverse nodes between i and j" / "reverse in groups of k"
process nodes tail-to-head (you have only forward pointers)
palindrome check or reorder (reverse the second half, then compare/merge)

picking.feature: The output is the SAME nodes with their link direction reversed or reordered, and O(1) extra space is demanded — rewire `next` with a prev/curr/nxt trio instead of copying values.

notWhen.because: the head is being spliced (inserted or removed), not turned around
you only need to FIND the middle or a cycle; reversal is the separate step that may follow

variants.title: Iterative template (prev / curr / next)
variants.code:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next     # SAVE next before you clobber it
        curr.next = prev    # flip
        prev = curr         # advance
        curr = nxt
    return prev             # new head

complexity.why: each node's `next` is flipped exactly once; three pointers

variants.title: Recursive template
variants.code:
def reverse(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = reverse(head.next)   # reverse the rest (trust it)
    head.next.next = head           # the node after me points back to me
    head.next = None                # I become the tail
    return new_head                 # relayed up unchanged

complexity.why: one call-stack frame per node — the recursion itself is the extra space

pitfalls: Clobbering `next` before saving it (iterative) — always `nxt = curr.next` first.
Recursive `head.next = None` omitted → the old head still points forward, creating a cycle.
Expecting `new_head` to change per frame — it doesn't; it's a pass-through payload. See recursion.

techniques.name: Intervals
techniques.whenToUse: Sort the intervals, then sweep left-to-right keeping a small piece of state.
signals: Intervals: "merge/insert overlapping" (→ a set)
Intervals: "max that fit" / "min to remove" / "min arrows" (→ a number)
"merge/combine overlapping intervals"
"insert an interval and merge"
"max intervals that fit" / "min to remove/erase"
"min rooms / max overlap / peak concurrency"
"does this new booking conflict?"

picking.feature: The sort key follows the goal, never the input: merging (the answer is a SET of intervals) sorts by START; scheduling (the answer is a NUMBER — keep / remove / count) sorts by END.

notWhen.because: the input is a contiguous run over one array, not a list of ranges to sort
you must count SIMULTANEOUS overlaps (meeting rooms II) — a min-heap of end times, not a merge

variants.title: Merge overlapping — sort by START
variants.when: collapse a set of intervals so no two overlap ("merge all overlapping intervals")
variants.code:
# 56 Merge Intervals
intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])          # by START
result = []
for start, end in intervals:
    if result and start <= result[-1][1]:   # overlaps the last kept interval
        result[-1][1] = max(result[-1][1], end)   # extend it (start is already <=, sorted)
    else:
        result.append([start, end])
return result

complexity.why: the sort dominates; the sweep is O(n) and the output holds up to n merged intervals

variants.title: Insert into a sorted interval list — the three-phase sweep
variants.when: a sorted, non-overlapping list is given; insert one new interval (57 Insert Interval)
variants.code:
# 57 Insert Interval
result, i, n = [], 0, len(intervals)
ns, ne = newInterval

# phase 1 — everything ending BEFORE the new one starts: copy untouched
while i < n and intervals[i][1] < ns:
    result.append(intervals[i]); i += 1

# phase 2 — everything overlapping: absorb by GROWING the new interval (no append)
while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= ne:
    ns = min(ns, intervals[i][0])
    ne = max(ne, intervals[i][1]); i += 1

# phase 3 — place the fully-grown interval ONCE, outside any loop
result.append([ns, ne])

# phase 4 — everything AFTER: copy the rest
while i < n:
    result.append(intervals[i]); i += 1
return result

complexity.why: the list is already sorted and non-overlapping, so no sort — one sweep with constant state beyond the output

variants.title: Interval scheduling — sort by END
variants.when: keep the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals, or (the mirror image) remove the minimum number so the rest don't overlap
variants.code:
# 435 Non-overlapping Intervals  (counts removals)
intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])          # by END
frontier, removed = float('-inf'), 0
for start, end in intervals:
    if start >= frontier:                   # no overlap → keep
        frontier = end
    else:                                    # overlaps → drop it
        removed += 1
return removed

complexity.why: sort by end, then one sweep holding only the current frontier end

pitfalls: Touching endpoints — is `[1,2]` vs `[2,3]` an overlap? It depends on the problem, and it is almost always stated. Use `<` vs `<=` accordingly. Getting this comparator wrong is the single most common interval bug.
The overlap comparator (`<` vs `<=`) is decided by the statement, not by habit. Touching endpoints are the classic off-by-one — check the problem's own example.

techniques.name: Monotonic Stack
techniques.whenToUse: A monotonic stack is a stack kept in sorted order (strictly/weakly increasing or decreasing) by popping any element that would break the order before pushing the new one. It answers "nearest greater/smaller element" queries for every element in O(n) total instead of O(n²).
signals: "next greater element" / "next smaller element"
"previous greater" / "previous smaller"
"days until a warmer temperature" (distance to next greater)
spans, or rectangle/area problems bounded by taller/shorter neighbors

picking.feature: For each element you need the NEAREST greater/smaller to one side — the stack discards anything that can never be an answer again, so every index is pushed and popped once.

notWhen.because: the question is the longest/shortest contiguous run meeting a condition, not a per-element nearest neighbour
you need the global max/min at any moment, not the nearest one per position

variants.title: The template
variants.code:
stack = []                                  # indices; values kept increasing bottom→top
for i, x in enumerate(arr):
    while stack and arr[stack[-1]] < x:      # x breaks the order → x is popped element's "next greater"
        idx = stack.pop()
        # arr[idx]'s next-greater is x, at distance (i - idx)
    stack.append(i)
# anything left on the stack has no next-greater element

complexity.why: every index is pushed once and popped at most once; the stack can hold all n on a sorted input

variants.title: Monotonic deque (moving-window max/min)
variants.code:
from collections import deque
dq = deque()                       # indices, values decreasing front→back
res = []
for i, x in enumerate(arr):
    while dq and arr[dq[-1]] < x:   # back: maintain monotonic order
        dq.pop()
    dq.append(i)
    if dq[0] <= i - k:              # front: evict out-of-window index
        dq.popleft()
    if i >= k - 1:
        res.append(arr[dq[0]])      # front = max of current window

complexity.why: each index enters and leaves the deque once; at most k indices are alive at a time

pitfalls: Storing values instead of indices — you lose the ability to compute distances/widths. Store indices, read `arr[idx]` when you need the value.

`<` vs `<=` — strict vs non-strict changes tie handling. For "next strictly greater," pop on `arr[top] < x`; for widths in histograms, the equal-height tie handling matters — reason it out per problem.
Forgetting leftovers — elements still on the stack at the end have no next-greater/smaller; handle them (often `-1` or the array boundary).
Wrong direction — "previous" queries iterate right→left (or check the stack before popping for the element that remains below).

techniques.name: Prefix Sum
techniques.whenToUse: A prefix sum array stores running totals so any range sum becomes a single subtraction. The high-leverage variant pairs prefix sums with a hashmap to answer "how many subarrays sum to k" in O(n).
signals: "sum of a subarray / range" — especially many range queries
"number of subarrays with sum == k" (or sum divisible by k)
"longest/shortest subarray summing to k"
any running-total or cumulative question

picking.feature: Many RANGE-SUM questions on a fixed array, or "how many subarrays sum to k" — a running total turns each range into one subtraction, and a hashmap of seen totals turns the count into a lookup.

notWhen.because: values are all non-negative and the question is longest/shortest run — the window is O(1) space and simpler; prefix + hashmap is what you reach for when negatives break the window

variants.title: Range sum queries
variants.code:
prefix = [0] * (len(arr) + 1)
for i, x in enumerate(arr):
    prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + x
# sum of arr[l..r] inclusive:
range_sum = prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]

complexity.why: one pass builds n + 1 running totals; each range query is a single subtraction

variants.title: Subarrays summing to k (prefix + hashmap)
variants.code:
count = 0
running = 0
seen = {0: 1}                 # prefix 0 seen once (empty prefix) — REQUIRED
for x in arr:
    running += x
    count += seen.get(running - k, 0)   # subarrays ending here that sum to k
    seen[running] = seen.get(running, 0) + 1
return count

complexity.why: one pass; the hashmap holds up to n distinct prefix totals

pitfalls: Forgetting `seen = {0: 1}` — without the empty-prefix seed, you miss subarrays that start at index 0.
Off-by-one — decide up front whether `prefix[i]` includes `arr[i]` or not, and keep the length-(n+1) convention to stay sane.
Counting vs length — "how many subarrays" stores counts in the map; "longest subarray" stores the first index a prefix was seen (so you maximize length).

techniques.name: Prim's — Minimum Spanning Tree
techniques.whenToUse: You have a connected weighted graph and want to keep every node reachable while paying as little total edge weight as possible.
signals: connect all points/nodes at minimum total cost
minimum cost to make all X connected
Weights given as coordinates rather than an edge list
Undirected + weighted + wants a structure, not a path

picking.feature: The objective is the cheapest set of edges that keeps EVERYTHING connected — a cost over the whole graph, not a distance from one source.

notWhen.because: the question is the cheapest ROUTE between nodes — a source-relative distance; an MST is not a shortest-path tree
Kruskal's (sort the edges, union-find) is the other MST — reach for it on a sparse edge list; Prim's O(V²) wins on a dense graph or a point set

variants.title: The procedure
variants.code:
def prim_mst(adj: list[list[int]]) -> int:      # adj[u][v] = weight; dense matrix input
    V = len(adj)
    in_tree = [False] * V
    best = [float('inf')] * V                    # cheapest known edge INTO each node from the tree
    best[0] = 0                                  # start anywhere
    total = 0
    for _ in range(V):
        u = min((v for v in range(V) if not in_tree[v]), key=lambda v: best[v])
        in_tree[u] = True
        total += best[u]                          # this edge joins the tree
        for v in range(V):                        # relax: is there a cheaper way INTO v now?
            if not in_tree[v] and adj[u][v] < best[v]:
                best[v] = adj[u][v]
    return total

complexity.why: V rounds, each doing two O(V) scans (find-the-min, then relax); the dist array plus the visited set.

pitfalls: Relax only unvisited nodes. A visited node's `dist` is already spent; letting it drop later corrupts the final `sum(dist)`.
`sum(dist)` is the answer precisely because `dist[i]` freezes at the moment `i` is picked, and `dist[0]` is 0. If either of those stops being true, the accumulator is wrong.
The start node is arbitrary. Any node gives a correct MST (possibly a different one of equal weight).
Negative weights are fine. Prim's compares edges; it never sums them into a path, so there's nothing for a negative edge to break. (This is the opposite of the shortest-path algorithms.)
Disconnected input ⟹ no spanning tree exists. 1584 can't hit this (a complete graph is always connected), but a general graph can: the min-picker would return a node whose `dist` is still ∞.
Ties don't matter. Any minimum-weight choice is fine; MSTs aren't unique when weights repeat.

keyProblems.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points

techniques.name: Recursion & Call Stack Traversal
techniques.whenToUse: The structure is self-similar (a list is a node plus a smaller list; a tree is a root plus subtrees) and the work at each node is the same — let the call stack carry the position instead of an explicit loop.
signals: Pipeline/Chain Construction
End-Relative Analytics

picking.feature: Where the work sits relative to the recursive call is the whole decision: BEFORE it (head / pre-order) when the current node decides what comes next; AFTER it (tail / post-order) when you need the answer from the end first.

notWhen.because: the structure is a TREE — same idea, but the pre / in / post vocabulary is the one to reason with
the recursion revisits the same state — add a cache or the call tree explodes

variants.title: Head Recursion (Pre-Order Execution)
variants.when: Building structural pipelines forward, or executing state evaluations on the way down toward the base case.
variants.code:
def mergeTwoLists(self, list1: ListNode, list2: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    # Base Case: If either list runs out, return the remaining pool
    if not list1: return list2
    if not list2: return list1
    
    # WORK HAPPENS FIRST: Compare current head elements
    if list1.val < list2.val:
        # Delegate remaining pipeline structure to the next frame
        list1.next = self.mergeTwoLists(list1.next, list2)
        return list1 # Return current node as the confirmed segment head
    else:
        list2.next = self.mergeTwoLists(list1, list2.next)
        return list2 # Return current node as the confirmed segment head

complexity.why: one frame per node of the merged output; the call stack is the extra space

variants.title: Tail Recursion (Post-Order Execution)
variants.when: Traversing to an unknown endpoint (like a tail pointer) first, then running evaluations backward relative to that end boundary.
variants.code:
def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: ListNode, n: int) -> ListNode:
    self.counter = 0 # Explicit global scope primitive to track return index
    
    def helper(node):
        if not node: return None # Base case: plant flag at the absolute tail
        
        # DIVING PHASE: Push frames forward until tail boundary is reached
        node.next = helper(node.next)
        
        # POPPING PHASE: This logic executes in reverse order on the way up
        self.counter += 1 
        if self.counter == n:
            return node.next # Drop target node by returning its successor pointer
            
        return node # Preserve untouched structural links
        
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    dummy.next = helper(head)
    return dummy.next

complexity.why: walks to the tail then unwinds — every node costs one frame

pitfalls: No base case, or a base case placed after the recursive call — the stack overflows before it is ever checked
Putting the work before the call when the answer needs the tail first (or vice versa) — the order of those two lines IS the algorithm
Python's recursion limit (~1000 frames) — a 10⁴-node list needs the iterative form
Mutating shared state (a counter, a list) across frames without meaning to — pass it explicitly or hold it on `self` on purpose

keyProblems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

techniques.name: Sliding Window
techniques.whenToUse: When a problem asks for the longest or shortest contiguous subarray or substring satisfying a condition, grow the right edge freely and shrink the left edge conditionally.
signals: "Contiguous subarray/substring" + a constraint (≤ k distinct, sum, longest/shortest)
Subarray of explicit static width `K`
Longest contiguous substring criteria
Smallest window containing specific items

picking.feature: A CONTIGUOUS run plus a condition that stays true (or false) as the window grows — that monotonicity is what lets the left edge only ever move right.

notWhen.because: values can be negative, or the question is "count subarrays summing to k" — the window cannot decide which edge to move; use prefix totals + a hashmap
the two indices are chosen from anywhere in a sorted array (a pair), not the two ends of one contiguous run

variants.title: Fixed Window Pattern
variants.when: Computing aggregate metrics across consecutive element windows of an exact static width k.
variants.code:
def find_max_average(nums: list[int], k: int) -> float:
    curr_sum = 0
    # Initialize first window prefix sum
    for i in range(k): curr_sum += nums[i]
    max_sum = curr_sum
    
    for r in range(k, len(nums)):
        curr_sum += nums[r] - nums[r - k]  # Add right, subtract left element
        max_sum = max(max_sum, curr_sum)
    return max_sum / k

complexity.why: each element is added once and subtracted once; a single running sum

variants.title: Dynamic Window (Max Variant)
variants.when: Seeking the maximum length sequence that satisfies a specific constraint configuration.

complexity.why: `r` visits each index once and `l` never moves back — at most 2n steps; the set holds the window's distinct characters, bounded by the alphabet Σ

variants.title: Dynamic Window (Min Variant)
variants.when: Locating the smallest possible localized footprint that fulfills the mandatory requirements.
variants.code:
def min_subarray_len(target: int, nums: list[int]) -> int:
    l, total = 0, 0
    min_len = float('inf')
    for r in range(len(nums)):
        total += nums[r]
        while total >= target:  # Condition valid: aggressively shrink window
            min_len = min(min_len, r - l + 1)
            total -= nums[l]
            l += 1
    return 0 if min_len == float('inf') else min_len

complexity.why: the same two-edge sweep; only a running total is kept

pitfalls: Updating the result inside the shrink loop instead of outside — misses valid states
Using a dict for counts but not deleting the key when count reaches zero — size check breaks
Conflating "at most k" vs "exactly k" — exactly k = (at most k) − (at most k−1)
Shrinking the window when it is already empty — guard with left <= right before shrinking

techniques.name: Topological Sort
techniques.whenToUse: A topological sort orders the nodes of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so every edge u → v has u before v. It answers "given dependencies, what's a valid order?" — and, as a side effect, detects cycles (a cyclic graph has no valid ordering).
signals: "prerequisites" / "dependencies" / "build order" / "course schedule"
"can you finish all tasks given these constraints?" (= is the graph a DAG?)
any "do A before B" ordering over a directed graph

picking.feature: A DIRECTED dependency graph and the question is an order (or whether one exists) — every edge u → v is a "u before v" constraint, and a cycle means no answer.

notWhen.because: edges are undirected and the question is connectivity, not order
the question is fewest steps, not a valid ordering — plain BFS without the indegree bookkeeping

variants.title: Kahn's algorithm (BFS on indegrees)
variants.when: Repeatedly remove nodes with no remaining prerequisites (indegree 0).
variants.code:
from collections import deque
indeg = [0] * n
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for u, v in edges:            # edge u -> v  (u must come before v)
    adj[u].append(v)
    indeg[v] += 1

q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
order = []
while q:
    u = q.popleft()
    order.append(u)
    for v in adj[u]:
        indeg[v] -= 1
        if indeg[v] == 0:
            q.append(v)

# if len(order) < n → a cycle exists (some nodes never hit indegree 0)
return order if len(order) == n else []

complexity.why: each node is enqueued once and each edge decremented once; adjacency lists plus the indegree array

variants.title: DFS postorder (reverse)
variants.when: Finish a node only after all its descendants; the reverse of finish order is a topo order.
variants.code:
WHITE, GRAY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2
color = [WHITE] * n
order = []
def dfs(u):
    color[u] = GRAY
    for v in adj[u]:
        if color[v] == GRAY:      # back edge → cycle
            return False
        if color[v] == WHITE and not dfs(v):
            return False
    color[u] = BLACK
    order.append(u)               # postorder
    return True
# run dfs on every WHITE node; final answer is order reversed

complexity.why: every node and edge is visited once; the colour array plus the recursion stack

pitfalls: Edge direction — `u -> v` means "u before v," so `v` gets the indegree. Reversing this silently breaks everything.
Forgetting the cycle check — Kahn's: `len(order) < n`; DFS: the GRAY (in-progress) state. Without it you return a bogus partial order.
Disconnected graphs — seed Kahn's queue with all indegree-0 nodes; run DFS from every unvisited node.

techniques.name: Tree BFS (Level-Order Traversal)
techniques.whenToUse: Visit nodes level by level using a queue. The trick that makes "per level" work is snapshotting the queue length at the start of each level.
signals: "level order" / "group values by depth"
shortest path / minimum depth (BFS finds the nearest first)
right/left side view, largest value per level, zigzag
anything "by distance from the root"

picking.feature: The question is PER LEVEL (widths, right-side view, zigzag) or FEWEST EDGES from the root — only a queue processes nodes in distance order.

notWhen.because: the parent's answer depends on the children's (height, diameter, validate) — that is postorder, and BFS has no notion of "children first"

variants.title: Template — the level-size snapshot
variants.code:
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    if not root: return []
    q = deque([root])
    result = []
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):     # snapshot: only THIS level's nodes
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:  q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)
        result.append(level)
    return result

complexity.why: each node is enqueued once; the queue holds one level at a time, up to the tree's maximum width w (≈ n/2 for a full tree)

pitfalls: `list.pop(0)` instead of `deque.popleft()` — `pop(0)` is O(n), making the whole traversal O(n²). Always use `collections.deque`.
Not snapshotting `len(q)` — if you loop `while q` without the inner `range(len(q))`, you can't tell where one level ends.
Forgetting the empty-root guard → `deque([None])` processes a phantom node.

keyProblems.title: Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row

techniques.name: Tree DFS (Depth-First Traversal)
techniques.whenToUse: Explore one branch fully before backtracking, via recursion (call stack) or an explicit stack. The order you process the node relative to its children — pre / in / post — is the whole choice.
signals: compute a property that depends on children (height, balanced, diameter) → postorder
need parent context available before children → preorder
need sorted output from a BST, or validate BST → inorder

picking.feature: The order is fixed by which way the information flows: POSTORDER when the parent's answer needs the children's answers first (height, balanced, diameter); INORDER when a BST must read out sorted (validate, kth-smallest).

notWhen.because: the question is level-by-level or minimum depth — depth-first walks a whole branch before the next, so levels blur

variants.title: The three orders (recursive)
variants.code:
def pre(node):   # Root, Left, Right
    if not node: return
    visit(node); pre(node.left); pre(node.right)

def ino(node):   # Left, Root, Right   — BST inorder = sorted ascending
    if not node: return
    ino(node.left); visit(node); ino(node.right)

def post(node):  # Left, Right, Root   — child results ready before parent
    if not node: return
    post(node.left); post(node.right); visit(node)

complexity.why: every node is visited once; the recursion depth is the tree height h (n in the worst, skewed case)

variants.title: Common DFS shapes
variants.code:
def height(node):                      # postorder
    if not node: return 0
    return 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))

def is_valid_bst(node, lo=float('-inf'), hi=float('inf')):
    if not node: return True
    if not (lo < node.val < hi): return False
    return (is_valid_bst(node.left, lo, node.val) and
            is_valid_bst(node.right, node.val, hi))

complexity.why: the same single visit per node; the bounds passed down add O(1) per frame

pitfalls: Missing the null base case → crash on leaf children.
Confusing "depth returned upward" with "answer tracked globally" — e.g. diameter is a local max at every node, separate from the height you return (543 trap).
Sentinel propagation — balanced-check returns `-1` for "unbalanced"; you must short-circuit on it before arithmetic (110 trap).
Recursion depth — O(h) stack; a skewed tree is O(n).

keyProblems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

techniques.name: Two Pointers
techniques.whenToUse: Use two pointers on a sorted array or string when searching for a pair, triplet, or re-arranging elements in-place — it collapses an O(n²) nested search to O(n).
signals: Sorted array + "find a pair/triple summing to target"
Sorted Sequence Pairs
Node Loop / Middle Node
In-place Content Removal

picking.feature: Sorted (or sortable) input where moving ONE index in a known direction can only change the comparison one way — that monotonic response is what lets two indices replace a nested loop.

notWhen.because: the pair must be a contiguous RUN, not two arbitrary positions
you need one boundary index, not a pair

variants.title: Opposite Ends Pattern
variants.when: Finding pairs or checking symmetries in sorted structural constraints.

complexity.why: the pointers close by at least one step per iteration

variants.title: Fast & Slow Pointer Pattern (Tortoise and Hare)
variants.when: Detecting structural loops, intersections, or calculating dynamic midpoints.

complexity.why: fast traverses the list in at most n/2 steps; two references

variants.title: Separation Pattern
variants.when: Modifying arrays in-place while separating elements based on content.

complexity.why: fast scans once; slow only advances on a keeper — in place

pitfalls: Applying two pointers to an unsorted array without sorting first — produces wrong results
Not skipping duplicate values in 3Sum — the output will contain duplicate triplets
Infinite loop from failing to advance a pointer after processing a match
Off-by-one: use left < right (not <=) when the pointers must not cross

keyProblems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted

techniques.name: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
techniques.whenToUse: Union-Find tracks a partition of elements into disjoint groups, supporting two near-O(1) operations: find (which group is x in?) and union (merge two groups). With path compression + union by rank, both are effectively O(α(n)) ≈ O(1).
signals: "are these two connected?" / "how many connected components?"
grouping / clustering elements as edges arrive (dynamic connectivity)
detecting a cycle in an undirected graph (union two already-connected nodes → cycle)
"redundant connection," "number of provinces," "accounts merge"
anything where you incrementally merge sets and query membership

picking.feature: Edges arrive ONE AT A TIME, or the only question is "are these two in the same group?" — union-find answers it in near-O(1) per edge without ever walking the graph.

notWhen.because: the graph is given whole and you need to WALK it (a path, an order, levels) — group membership alone is not the question
edges are directed and the question is order, not connectivity

variants.title: Template

complexity.why: With path compression + union by rank, both find and union are effectively O(α(n)) ≈ O(1); the parent and rank arrays are the only state

pitfalls: Skipping path compression — without it, `find` degrades to O(n) and trees get tall.
Union without checking roots first — always `find` both and compare roots before merging.
1D index mapping for grids — flatten `(r, c)` → `r * cols + c`. Use `cols` (width) for the stride and `col` for the offset — mixing `rows`/`cols` here is the 130 typo trap.
Forgetting the dummy node — border/"escape" problems (130) union everything on the border to one extra sentinel node, then check who shares its root.
